_as_float silently maps any non-int/float value to 0.0. That includes np.float32, which is not a float subclass, and numpy types are used elsewhere in this package. Such values become fake zero-energy frames that can pollute the baseline or cause false flags. The issue only asks that missing keys count as 0.0. Use float(value) and let bad types raise, or accept numbers.Real.

update() calls _reevaluate(), which re-evaluates every speaker and, for each candidate, scans all peers. That is O(n²) per snapshot and redoes window means for speakers that did not change. This is fine for small groups. Caching window means, or only re-evaluating the updated speaker plus currently flagged ones, would be cheaper.

`_peer_engaged` ignores any peer that is not `ready`, meaning fewer than 10 updates or fewer than 10 window entries. A speaker who has been steady for a few updates, or who joined late, can never count as 'still engaged'. A real one-sided drop is then missed whenever the only other speaker has short history, which matches no wording in the spec. Decide this explicitly. For example, use whatever baseline and window the peer has, or document the requirement. Add a test for the two-speaker case where the peer has little history.

The EMA baseline updates on every unflagged sample, including the dropped samples that are still being judged. A gradual or stepped decline therefore drags the baseline down before the flag trips. The ratios are compared against a contaminated baseline, and a slow fade may never cross 60% / 40%. The freeze only applies once flagged, which is too late. Consider updating the baseline only from samples that are not clearly below it, or lagging the baseline update behind the window. At minimum, state this tradeoff.

The first 10 samples form the baseline and also fill the first window. The first readiness check therefore compares the baseline with its own data. This is harmless but redundant. Separately, group-lull protection depends on the peer's window lagging by at most about one update. A staggered lull, where peers drop a few updates after the first speaker, will flag the first speaker. That is permanent until recovery because of hysteresis. Worth a note or a test.

`_reevaluate` runs over all speakers on every `update`. Each pass recomputes `recent_means` and calls `_peer_engaged`, which is O(n²·window) per update. Only the updated speaker's own metrics change, so only its decision and its peers' dependency on its engagement need recomputing. Fine at small speaker counts, wasteful on a hot path. Cache the window sums in `_SpeakerState`.

`float(features.get(...) or 0.0)` lets NaN or inf through. A NaN in the baseline sum permanently makes `baseline_usable` False, so that speaker is silently never flagged. Sanitize non-finite values to 0.0, or document the behaviour.

`MIN_BASELINE = 1e-6` is an absolute cutoff shared by energy (about 0.1) and F0 std (about 30 Hz). 'Near-zero' therefore means different things for the two metrics. Consider separate thresholds, or document the unit assumption.

Flags are latched per update, so the outcome depends on update order. If sp0 drops first while sp1 is still normal, sp0 is flagged and stays flagged under hysteresis. When sp1 then drops, the flagged sp0 no longer counts as an engaged peer, so sp1 is not flagged either. The result is sp0 alone flagged after a group lull, which violates 'if every speaker goes quiet together, nobody is flagged'. Uneven update rates cause the same thing, because windows count updates, not time. The flag also never re-checks that a flagged speaker still has an engaged peer. Evaluate the peer condition against current state at query time, or re-evaluate and clear flags that no longer have an engaged peer.

`baseline_usable` uses an absolute 1e-6 cutoff and requires both energy and F0 baselines to clear it. A speaker with a real energy baseline but a zero F0 baseline is never flagged, and as a peer never counts as engaged. Choose a threshold that fits the feature scale and document it.

The baseline EMA keeps adapting during the roughly 9 drop updates before the flag latches. In the issue's example this pulls the energy baseline from 0.10 to about 0.087 and makes the recovery threshold more lenient. Delay adaptation, or skip updates that are already below the flag ratios.

`_reevaluate` runs for every speaker on every update, and `_peer_engaged` scans all peers each time, recomputing window means. That is O(n²) per update. Fine for small groups, but caching the means or evaluating lazily would remove it.

Baseline adaptation is skipped for every 'low' sample and for the whole time a speaker is flagged. A speaker who permanently settles at a quieter level is compared with the stale baseline forever, so the baseline never re-learns. That contradicts 'adapts slowly'. Freezing only while flagged would be enough. Otherwise document the limitation or add a bounded re-baseline.

MIN_BASELINE = 1e-6 is an absolute threshold for 'near-zero'. A very quiet speaker with a baseline energy of around 1e-5 to 1e-4 passes the check and can be flagged on noise. The issue says a near-zero baseline must never be flagged. Use a larger floor, or document why this value is chosen.

If one speaker's quiet window fills first (uneven or sequential updates), they are flagged while the others look normal. When the others then go quiet, the flag persists, so a group lull ends up flagging someone. Re-check peer engagement for held flags, or clear the flag when no peer is engaged. The _reevaluate comment is garbled. The method also re-evaluates all speakers on every update, with a nested peer scan and window re-sums, which is O(n²·window) per update. Limit the recheck to what changed, or keep running sums.

A peer with energy but missing or zero f0_std can never count as engaged, so the flag is suppressed incorrectly. The baseline is frozen while flagged, so a speaker who settles at a new quieter level stays flagged forever. The spec says the baseline adapts slowly, not that it freezes. This is an undocumented behavioural decision. Either document it or let the baseline adapt very slowly while flagged.

`count` keeps incrementing after warm-up but is only compared against BASELINE_SNAPSHOTS. Cap it or replace it with a warmed-up bool.

`float(features.get(k, 0.0) or 0.0)` passes NaN through (`nan or 0.0` is NaN). One NaN snapshot makes the cumulative baseline NaN, so `baseline_valid` stays false and that speaker is never flagged and never counted as a peer. Sanitize non-finite values to 0.0 or skip the snapshot.

If it is intended, add a docstring line saying so.

`update()` calls `_reevaluate()`, which re-checks every speaker, and each unflagged candidate scans all other speakers in `_peer_engaged`. That is O(n²) per snapshot, and one speaker's update can change other speakers' flags. The speaker count is small, so it is probably fine. A comment saying the cross-speaker re-evaluation is deliberate (a peer's state can enable or disable a flag) would help the next reader.

`ready` checks both `count >= BASELINE_UPDATES` and `len(window) >= WINDOW_SIZE`. Both constants are 10, so the two checks are redundant. If they are meant to be independent, say so. Otherwise reduce to one check. The `else: flagged = False` reset in `_reevaluate` also looks unreachable after warm-up.

`damping_factor` is not validated, so a value outside [0, 1] would amplify or negate the rapport instead of scaling it down. This is optional and probably out of scope, so a docstring line documenting the expected range would be enough.

The peer-engaged condition is checked only when raising a flag. Once sp0 is flagged, flagged speakers are excluded from `_peer_engaged`, so sp1 is never flagged when it also goes quiet, and sp0's flag also never clears. A group lull that starts with a lag, or with updates fed per-speaker rather than interleaved, therefore leaves one speaker permanently flagged. The issue requires that nobody is flagged when everyone goes quiet together. Re-check the peer condition for flagged speakers, or clear a flag when no engaged peer remains.

The baseline is frozen while `st.flagged`. A speaker who settles at a level between the flag thresholds and the 70% recovery threshold stays flagged indefinitely, because the baseline never adapts and the window mean never reaches 70%. Decide whether this is intended, and document it or allow very slow adaptation while flagged.

Baseline adaptation is frozen while flagged, and samples under 60% energy / 40% F0 std are skipped even when unflagged. The issue says the baseline 'adapts slowly'. This version can't follow a lasting level change or re-baseline after a long group lull. It also biases the baseline upward over time. Quiet speakers then keep blocking each other as engaged peers and keep stale flags. Decide this deliberately and document it, or adapt on all unflagged samples.

A flagged speaker stays flagged through a later group-wide lull because the peer-engaged condition is only checked for new flags. That is defensible hysteresis, but it is unstated and depends on update ordering. Document it or handle it explicitly.

PEER_NORMAL_RATIO = 0.8 is an invented threshold. The issue only says 'near their own normal energy'. It sits between the 0.6 flag and 0.7 recovery ratios, so a peer at 70-79% of baseline does not count as engaged. Align it with an existing ratio or call out the choice.

ForgeStreamConfig.rapport_damping_factor = 0.3 already exists, but the detector hard-codes its own 0.3 default and nothing connects them. The two can drift apart. Use the config value or have the caller pass it in.

_clean coerces NaN, inf, negative, and non-numeric values to 0.0, which goes beyond 'missing keys count as 0.0' and can make bad upstream data look like disengagement. Drop non-finite samples instead. Also, _reevaluate recomputes window means for all speakers on every update, and _peer_engaged makes that O(n^2) per update. Caching the means is cheap.

Flags depend on update order. If one speaker's quiet snapshots arrive before the others start dropping, that speaker is flagged while the rest still look normal. The flag is sticky, so it persists after everyone goes quiet. The spec says a group lull flags nobody. Re-check the peer condition on later updates, or clear flags when no peer is engaged.

_peer_engaged requires usable_baseline, which needs both the energy and F0 baselines above MIN_BASELINE. The peer test only uses energy, so a peer with no f0_std data can never count as engaged. It should check only the energy baseline.
The baseline is frozen while flagged and only 70% recovery clears the flag. A speaker who settles at about 65% of baseline stays flagged forever. Decide whether that is intended and document it.
_clean silently maps NaN, inf, negative and non-numeric values to 0.0, which counts as very low energy. This is unrequested and hides upstream bugs. The spec only says missing keys count as 0.0.
MIN_BASELINE = 1e-6 is an arbitrary absolute cutoff with no stated scale reasoning. Explain it or derive it from typical energy_rms.

Baseline adaptation is skipped while `st.flagged`, and a flag is only cleared at 70% or more of the frozen baseline. A speaker whose normal level settles at 60–70% of the old baseline therefore stays flagged indefinitely. The same holds if the whole group goes quiet after the flag was raised. This matches the hysteresis spec, but it has no escape path and no comment. Add a comment, or decide on a bound such as slow adaptation toward the window mean while flagged.

`PEER_NORMAL_RATIO = 0.8` is an invented threshold. The spec says only 'near their own normal energy level', and nothing documents or justifies 0.8. It decides whether a flag is raised at all, so a peer at 70–79% blocks flagging. Say in a comment that this is a tunable choice. Consider making it a constructor argument.

`usable_baseline` requires both `energy_base` and `f0_base` to be at least `MIN_BASELINE`. A speaker whose snapshots never carry `f0_std` (it defaults to 0.0) is therefore never flagged, and also never counts as an engaged peer. That is a silent behaviour choice the spec doesn't state. Likewise, a peer with a zero baseline is excluded from `engaged`, so a lone remaining speaker with a degenerate baseline suppresses flagging for everyone else. Document it, or make the baseline check per metric.

The detector isn't connected to anything. `config.py` already defines `rapport_damping_factor = 0.3`, and the constructor default repeats the same value. Nothing feeds `PROSODIC_FEATURE` events into `update()`, and nothing applies `get_pair_damping` to the rapport composite. The issue's stated purpose is scaling the rapport composite, so either wire it in (or state that this is deliberate follow-up work) or at least source the default from the config to avoid two copies of 0.3.

`_reevaluate` runs on every `update()` and recomputes `window_means()` twice per speaker (once for `engaged`, once in the loop). That costs O(speakers × window) per snapshot. Compute the means once per speaker, or cache them in the state when appending.

The warmup samples also fill the sliding window, so `ready` becomes true exactly when the baseline is set (both thresholds are 10). The baseline and the first 'recent' window are then identical, which isn't obvious. A one-line comment would help. `BASELINE_WARMUP` and `WINDOW_SIZE` are separate constants that are implicitly coupled.

Peer engagement is checked only when a flag is raised, and the only exit is recovery. If a flagged speaker's peers later go quiet too, nobody is engaged any more, but the flag stays and `get_pair_damping` keeps damping. The issue says a group lull flags nobody. Either re-check peers (unflag when no peer is engaged) or document and test the sticky behaviour.

`damping_factor` is unvalidated, so negative or >1 values would silently scale rapport up or negative. `Config.rapport_damping_factor` already holds the same 0.3 default but nothing reads it. Consider a range check, or note who passes the config value in.

Baseline EMA is updated with each snapshot before it is judged, so it drifts toward the drop being detected. In the issue's example the energy baseline falls from 0.10 to about 0.091 and F0 std from 30 to about 27 by the time the flag is set. That shifts the 60%/40%/70% thresholds, so borderline recoveries clear the flag. Hold or skip the baseline update while the window is below the drop thresholds, or build the baseline from samples older than the judging window.

`elif not self.flagged` freezes baseline adaptation while flagged. A speaker who settles at a new lower level (about 50% of baseline) never reaches the 70% recovery threshold and stays flagged forever. The spec says the baseline adapts slowly, with no exception for flagged speakers. Keep slow adaptation while flagged, or document and bound the freeze.

The peer-engaged condition is only checked when setting the flag. Once flagged, a speaker stays flagged even if every other speaker also goes quiet and flat, which the issue calls a group lull where nobody is flagged. It is also order-dependent: if speakers drop sequentially rather than interleaved, the first one is flagged while the others are still normal and is never un-flagged. Re-check the peer condition for flagged speakers on each update, or clear the flag, or stop reporting it, when no peer is near normal energy.
The `if not state.ready: state.flagged = False` branch only triggers if the baseline decays to the floor or below. Add a short comment, or drop the reset if it is unintended.

A flag is never re-checked against the 'another speaker still near normal' condition once set. It clears only on recovery. In a staggered lull (or when speakers are updated sequentially rather than interleaved), the first speaker to go quiet stays flagged after everyone else goes quiet too. That contradicts 'group lull flags nobody'. Decide whether a flag should drop when no peer is near normal, and add a test for staggered ordering.

near_normal uses each peer's last window with no recency. A speaker who stopped sending updates (left the call) counts as 'near normal' forever and keeps enabling flags on the others. Expire stale peers or document that all speakers must update continuously.

The baseline is frozen while flagged. A speaker whose level settles between the flag and recovery thresholds (e.g. energy 0.065 vs. a 0.07 recovery bar) stays flagged indefinitely and the baseline never re-learns. Document this or add a bounded adaptation path.

The `if not st.ready or not st.usable: st.flagged = False` branch in _reevaluate is effectively unreachable, because readiness is monotonic and a frozen baseline can't become unusable after flagging. Remove it or comment it as a safety net.
The module constants lack rationale. MIN_BASELINE=1e-6 is arbitrary relative to the raw energy_rms scale, and the baseline-building and evaluation windows overlap at 10 updates. Add brief comments.

A flagged speaker's baseline is frozen (`not st.flagged` gate in `update`) and recovery is measured against that frozen baseline. If a speaker's normal level has really shifted down, the baseline never re-learns and the flag never clears. The same freeze applies to a non-flagged speaker during a group lull, because the gate skips adaptation for any low snapshot. Consider a bounded re-baselining path, or document that this is intended. The issue does say 'adapts slowly'.
`__all__` is alphabetical. `DisengagementDetector` sorts before `EGeMAPSExtractor`, not after `EmotionCorrelator`.

Group-lull detection depends on the order of updates. `_reevaluate` runs after every single `update()`, and the flag is sticky. If speakers go quiet in sequence (A's low snapshots arrive before B's, or the lull is staggered), A can pass the check while B's window still has energy ratio >= 0.7. A is then flagged and stays flagged by hysteresis, even after B also goes quiet. The issue says 'if every speaker goes quiet and flat together, nobody is flagged'. In the interleaved case the margin is thin: at the step where `sp0`'s F0 criterion is first met, `sp1` has energy ratio about 0.64 against the 0.7 cutoff. Fix: judge the peer against a state that cannot be skewed by ordering. For example, require the drop to persist for a full window while a peer stays engaged. Or let a flag be withdrawn while all speakers are quiet and no peer has been engaged.

The baseline is only frozen once `flagged` is set, but the flag needs a full window of low values. Throughout the decline, the EMA (`BASELINE_ALPHA * (energy - base)`) is pulling the baseline toward the lull. This erodes the thresholds the speaker is about to be judged against. A group lull erodes everyone's baseline too, so afterwards a normal-level speaker looks 'recovered'. Fix: freeze or slow baseline updates when the new snapshot is below the drop thresholds, or update the baseline from samples leaving the window rather than entering it.

A NaN or inf in `energy_rms` or `f0_std` goes through `float(... or 0.0)` unchanged (NaN is truthy). It poisons the running mean and EMA permanently, so `ready` stays False and that speaker is never flagged and never counts as a peer. Praat extraction can produce NaN for unvoiced frames. Treat non-finite values as 0.0 or skip them.

`_peer_engaged` uses a separate 0.7 threshold, `PEER_ENGAGED_RATIO`. The spec only says 'near their own normal energy level'. It also silently ignores peers that are not `ready`. A peer with fewer than 10 updates or a zero baseline never counts as engaged, so no one is flagged in a two-person call with a new or silent peer. This is defensible but undocumented. Add a docstring or comment stating the intent.

`_reevaluate` loops over every speaker and recomputes both window sums, and `_peer_engaged` does so again for each candidate, on every `update()`. That is O(n²) per snapshot. Evaluate only the updated speaker, plus peers whose state could change, or keep running sums for the windows.

The baseline EMA keeps updating on every unflagged snapshot after warm-up, including the low snapshots that precede a flag. That erodes the baseline before the flag fires and during any group lull, because the freeze applies only while flagged. In the issue's example the energy baseline falls from 0.10 to about 0.088 and the F0 baseline from 30 to about 26.3 by the time `sp0` is flagged. Recovery then clears against the eroded baseline: energy 0.065 reads as 0.73 of baseline and clears, although it is only 65% of the true 0.10. Fix by adapting the baseline only from snapshots that are not depressed, for example when the window ratios are above the drop thresholds. Alternatively, keep the pre-drop baseline for the recovery check.

`_reevaluate()` runs after every `update()` and re-sums both windows for every speaker, and `_peer_engaged` re-sums them again per candidate. That is O(N²·W) per snapshot, when only the updated speaker's window changed. Evaluate only `speaker_id`. Peer readiness changes only when a peer's own update arrives, so one speaker's update never needs to re-flag a different speaker. Alternatively, cache the running sums.

Flags live in `_SpeakerState.flagged`, but the repo's Task 3 plan (docs/superpowers/plans/2026-03-29-rapport-tracking.md) tests damping by setting `det._flags["sp0"] = True` and expecting `get_pair_damping("sp0","sp1") == 0.3`. This PR has no `_flags`, so that test raises. Either keep a `_flags: dict[str, bool]` as the single source of truth for flag state, or update the plan and its test to match. As written the planned test cannot pass.

The flag latches the moment a speaker's window crosses the thresholds while another speaker's window is still engaged. If streams are not in lockstep, a real group lull gets a false flag. Example: sp0 sends 12 low snapshots before sp1 sends any. sp0 is flagged against sp1's old steady window and stays flagged through hysteresis even after sp1 goes quiet. The test pattern in the plan interleaves updates, so it hides this. Mitigations: require the 'others engaged' condition to hold for several consecutive evaluations, or clear a flag when no other speaker is engaged any more. Otherwise document that updates must be interleaved.

Constants drift from the repo's rapport design spec: it says last 10 events (code uses WINDOW_SIZE=8) and baseline EMA alpha=0.01 (code uses 0.02). The spec also requires a negative energy-slope check, and that check is absent. The issue text doesn't mention the slope, so either align the constants with the spec or note the deviation.

If the first BASELINE_UPDATES snapshots give a zero or near-zero baseline, `_update_baseline` returns early on `not st.usable_baseline` and the baseline never adapts. The speaker can never be flagged, and the baseline does not recover if they start speaking normally. That is safe for the no-divide-by-zero requirement but permanent. Consider letting the baseline keep accumulating until it becomes usable.

`_others_engaged` skips any speaker whose `f0_base` is unusable. A speaker with a healthy energy baseline but missing `f0_std` (counts as 0.0) therefore never counts as 'still engaged', even though the 'others' condition is defined on energy only. Gate the other-speaker check on `energy_base` alone.

`ready` checks `len(self.window) == WINDOW_SIZE`, which is redundant once `energy_base` is set because baseline needs 10 updates and the window is 8. The repeated `assert ... is not None` lines only narrow types. Storing the baseline as one `tuple[float, float] | None` removes the asserts and the paired-None states.
MIN_BASELINE = 1e-6 is tiny for RMS energy. A near-silent speaker with a baseline around 1e-4 counts as usable and can be flagged. Raise it, or document the units it assumes.
NaN energy or f0 is not guarded. It permanently poisons that speaker's baseline, so they are never flagged and no error is raised. Sanitize non-finite values in update().
_reevaluate runs on every update and recomputes window means for every other speaker inside _others_engaged, so each update costs O(n²·W). Cache the window means or sums.
Repeated `assert ... is not None` calls only exist to satisfy the type checker and duplicate usable_baseline. Use non-optional floats plus a has_baseline flag instead.
"DisengagementDetector" is placed before "AudioRingBuffer" in __all__, which breaks the alphabetical order.

Add a docstring note that a flagged speaker stays flagged until their own recovery, even if the rest of the group later goes quiet. Also note that a speaker who never supplies f0_std is never flagged.

_reevaluate only requires an engaged peer when a speaker becomes flagged. After that, only the speaker's own recovery clears the flag. If speaker A is flagged while B is still normal, then B also goes quiet, A stays flagged although everyone is now quiet. That is the group-lull case the issue says must flag nobody. It shows up with staggered or sequential updates. Clear flags when no engaged peer remains, or at least document and test this behaviour. I did not run anything, so this is not confirmed as the cause of the hidden-test failure.

_is_engaged uses `judgeable`, which also requires f0_baseline > MIN_BASELINE. The issue defines a peer as engaged by energy alone. A peer with normal energy but a zero F0 baseline, such as unvoiced frames or a missing f0_std, is never counted as engaged, so a real disengagement next to that peer is missed. Check only the energy baseline for the peer test.

The baseline is frozen while a speaker is flagged, so a speaker whose real level settles lower stays flagged until they exceed 70% of the old baseline. This is deliberate and commented, and I would keep it. Document it in the class docstring so consumers of `get_pair_damping` know the flag can persist.

`_reevaluate` recomputes `recent_ratios()` and the window sums for every speaker on every update. `_is_engaged` computes them once and the main loop computes them again. Compute the ratios once per speaker per pass.

Flag state is a private `set` named `_flagged`. The repo's rapport plan (docs/superpowers/plans/2026-03-29-rapport-tracking.md, Step 1) has `test_get_damping_for_pair` set `det._flags["sp0"] = True` on a `dict[str, bool]` called `_flags`. With this PR that test raises AttributeError. Either keep the planned `_flags: dict[str, bool]` state, or update the plan and tests to a public way of forcing a flag.

The group-lull guard is not robust. `_reevaluate` judges the other speakers using whatever is in their windows right now. A speaker who has stopped being updated, such as someone who left or is not speaking, keeps their last 'normal' window indefinitely. That speaker satisfies `OTHER_NORMAL` for good, so a lull among the remaining speakers flags them. Updates are also event-driven and uneven per speaker. A speaker can cross the thresholds while another speaker's window has not caught up yet, and that flags them. The flag is then sticky because of the hysteresis. Decide how to treat stale or lagging speakers, for example by comparing only against speakers updated recently. Document the choice.
`DisengagementDetector` is not imported or added to `__all__`. Every other public class in the emotion package is exported there.

The baseline keeps adapting until the flag is set. During the roughly 9 updates it takes the window to cross the F0 threshold, the baseline drifts toward the depressed values, which is about 12–15% in the issue's example. That makes flagging slightly easier and recovery easier than the stated 'baseline'. Consider freezing the baseline whenever the window ratio is already below the enter thresholds, not only once the speaker is flagged.

`OTHER_NORMAL = 0.8` is a new threshold the issue does not define. The plan used the 0.6 energy threshold for 'other is normal'. Keep 0.8 if intended, but note the choice in a comment. Also, an already-flagged speaker whose energy has recovered but whose F0 has not can still count as 'another speaker still normal'.

DisengagementDetector is not imported or added to __all__. Sibling public classes (GroupDynamicsEngine, SpeakerTimeSeries, etc.) are all exported from the package, so consumers would have to import from the submodule.
_reevaluate recomputes every speaker's window means on every update, and the any(...) rescans the other speakers' ratios. That is O(S^2*W) per update. It is fine for small S but easy to simplify.

Group-lull rule is order- and arrival-dependent. If sp0's window goes quiet before sp1's, sp0 is flagged while sp1 still looks normal. When sp1 later goes quiet, sp0 stays flagged because the hysteresis path only checks recovery and never re-checks the group condition. Updates are per speaker and not synchronised, so staggered or block-wise updates flag someone in what is really a group lull. Compare speakers over a common recent horizon, or re-evaluate the 'others normal' condition when a flag is still set.
`normal` counts any peer whose last window is near baseline, even if that peer stopped updating long ago. A stale peer can vouch indefinitely and cause flags. Add a recency/staleness criterion.

The baseline EMA keeps updating on every non-flagged snapshot, so a gradual decline erodes the baseline before the 60% and 40% thresholds trip, and the flag may never fire. A speaker with a zero baseline after warm-up can also have it grow above EPS through the EMA and become flaggable later. The spec says zero-baseline speakers must never be flagged.

`WINDOW` serves as both the recent-window length and the baseline warm-up length. They are coupled (at n == WINDOW the window equals the baseline), so tuning one silently changes the other. Split the constants or document the coupling. The comment 'Energy ratios of speakers…' above `normal` also describes a set of IDs, not ratios.

Baseline is only frozen once flagged, so during the ~9 updates before the flag fires the EMA already erodes it (F0 30 -> ~26.3, energy 0.10 -> ~0.088 in the issue example). Recovery (70%) and drop (60%/40%) thresholds are then judged against a shrunken baseline, so hysteresis is looser than specified. A slow slide into silence also drags the baseline down and may never be flagged. Update the baseline from samples leaving the recent window, or freeze it while recent values are below the drop thresholds.
No tests for the new detector. The issue example, group lull, hysteresis and zero-baseline behaviours are all uncovered.
DisengagementDetector is not exported in __init__/__all__ like the sibling emotion classes. The constructor default 0.3 also duplicates Config.rapport_damping_factor and nothing connects the two.

A peer with fewer than WINDOW snapshots or a zero baseline never counts as 'near normal', so a speaker can't be flagged while the only other speaker is still warming up. This is a defensible reading of the issue, but undocumented.
Comment 'Energy ratios of speakers…' above `normal` is wrong: it is a set of speaker IDs. recent() is also recomputed twice per speaker on every update; consider caching or running sums.

The baseline is frozen for as long as `flagged` is True (`elif not self.flagged`). A speaker whose new steady level sits between the enter and recover thresholds, say energy at 65% of baseline, can then never clear. This also contradicts the 'then adapts slowly' requirement, because a flagged speaker never adapts. Clearing then depends only on the frozen pre-drop baseline. Keep adapting while flagged, or add an explicit bound, and cover this with a test.

Until the flag trips, every low snapshot is folded into the baseline with `BASELINE_ALPHA` (about 13% drift over the 7 updates it takes to flag). Detection is therefore judged against a baseline that is already contaminated by the drop. The baseline should lag the window, for example by updating from samples that have left the window. A slow decline can also pull the baseline down with it and never flag. In the issue's example the margin is still sufficient, but it is thin for borderline drops.

`_refresh()` runs on every `update()` for every speaker, and it clears `flagged` for any speaker that is not ready. Flag state therefore depends on other speakers' update ordering. A speaker flagged while a peer is still normal stays flagged after that peer goes quiet, because hysteresis only checks recovery. That is arguably correct, but the 'group lull' semantics for staggered drops are unspecified and untested. Document the behaviour.

`EPS = 1e-6` as the zero-baseline cutoff is unit-dependent. `energy_rms` here is roughly 0 to 0.15, so a very quiet but real baseline of around 1e-5 would still be flagged. Add a comment on the chosen units or a more meaningful floor. The module constants are also not tunable, while `config.py` already carries `rapport_damping_factor`. Nothing passes that value to the detector yet, but wiring was not requested.

A group lull can leave a speaker flagged. In `_refresh`, the `peer_ok` check applies only when entering the flagged state. If `sp0` is flagged while `sp1` is still normal and `sp1` then goes quiet and flat, `sp0` stays flagged by hysteresis, because the clear condition looks only at `sp0`'s own recovery. Updates arrive per speaker, so drops are rarely simultaneous, and this staggered case breaks the rule that a whole-group lull flags nobody. Fix: when no other speaker is near normal, clear the flag. Hysteresis should apply only to the recovery thresholds, not to the peer condition.

Peer normality has no staleness handling. A peer who stops sending updates keeps its last window and counts as 'still normal' indefinitely. That can keep a quiet speaker flagged, or flag one, because of a departed peer. The window is also not time-aware. Either document this limitation or drop stale peers.

The baseline keeps adapting toward the dropped values while a speaker is unflagged but already declining, and it is frozen once flagged. Between the start of a drop and the flag, about 7 updates pull the baseline down by roughly 10%. A speaker who stays quiet is never re-baselined. This is acceptable for a slow EMA, but the freeze-on-flag behaviour is a design choice that should be stated in the module docstring.

`_refresh` recomputes ratios for every speaker on every `update`, which costs O(speakers × WINDOW) each time. It also mutates `flagged` for speakers other than the one just updated. Refreshing only after the updated speaker's window changes, or caching the ratios, would be cheaper and clearer. Separately, the magic thresholds are module constants, which is fine, but `damping_factor` is not validated.

The `htmlBytes` doc says it only feeds the crawl window's memory-pressure signal and is capped at MAX_HTML_BYTES. It is now also reported for blocked/non-HTML pages, and the window uses it as a byte budget rather than a heavy-page trouble flag. Update the comment to say it is the buffered body size for any fetched page, and 0 for redirects and fetch errors.

`emptyPageResult` now requires `htmlBytes`, so the redirect and catch call sites each pass a literal `htmlBytes: 0`. An optional `htmlBytes` field defaulting to 0 would leave those two sites untouched and only the blocked/error site setting it.

`emptyPageResult` now takes a required `htmlBytes`, so the redirect and catch branches each pass `htmlBytes: 0` by hand. Only the blocked/error branch has a real value. Make it optional and default to 0 (`input.htmlBytes ?? 0`), which leaves two call sites untouched.

`persistChain` is pushed into `Promise.race` while paused. If a persist batch rejects, the race rejects mid-loop and the loop exits with fetches still in flight. Before, a persist failure only surfaced at the final `await persistChain`. Race on `persistChain.catch(() => {})` instead, so errors still surface at the final await.

`htmlBytes` is now a required `emptyPageResult` input, but the redirect and catch call sites pass a literal `0` because no body was read. Making it optional with a default of 0 would leave those sites untouched, and only the blocked/non-HTML site would pass `body.length`.

Persist failures now surface early. The race over `queuedPersists` rejects mid-loop, where before a rejected `persistChain` only surfaced at `await persistChain` after all fetches drained. The new path throws out of `runCrawlChunk` while fetches are still in flight and before `releaseUrls` runs for unlaunched leases. This is probably fine because the step retries and claims are idempotent, but it is an unstated behaviour change. Either confirm it is intended or swallow it in the race and let `await persistChain` surface it.

`emptyPageResult` now requires `htmlBytes`, and the redirect and catch sites pass a literal `0`. Make the field optional with a default of 0 so only the blocked path sets it. Also, `body.length` counts UTF-16 code units, not bytes, so the `htmlBytes` name and the byte budget are approximate for non-ASCII pages. That already applies to the ok path, so it is not new.

The idle-while-backlogged branch repeats the `nextIndex < claimed.length && Date.now() < deadlineAt` guards from the launch loop and adds its own `await persistChain; continue`. You could unify it: when backlogged, always race `[...inFlight, persistChain]`, and break only when `inFlight.size === 0` and launching was not held back. This is optional; the current logic is correct.

The `htmlBytes` doc comment still says it feeds the crawl window's 'memory-pressure signal'. It now feeds the in-flight HTML byte budget and is also populated for blocked and error pages, so the wording could be updated.

Adding `queuedPersists` to `Promise.race` changes failure timing. A rejected persist now makes the race reject, so `runCrawlChunk` throws mid-chunk while the other fetches are still in flight. Before this change, a persist rejection only surfaced at the final `await persistChain`. The in-flight promises are left running, and any rejection they raise is unobserved. The failure is probably fatal for the chunk either way, so this is likely fine. If not, race against `persist.catch(() => {})` and let the final `await persistChain` throw.

`htmlBytes` is optional on `emptyPageResult` and defaults to 0, so the redirect and catch callers silently rely on that default. That is correct today, because those paths have no body. Requiring the field would force each caller to state it. Separately, `body.length` counts UTF-16 code units, not bytes. This matches the existing OK path, but the name and doc comment on `htmlBytes` say bytes.

Racing `persistChain` while paused means a persist failure now rejects the crawl loop immediately, with fetches still in flight. Before, it only surfaced at the final `await persistChain`. Likely fine and arguably better, but it is an undocumented change in failure timing. Confirm it is intended.

While paused, `Promise.race([...inFlight, persistChain])` waits for the whole persist chain to finish, not for the queue to drop to the limit. Fetching sits idle until every queued sub-batch is written, which is slightly more conservative than 'stop while more than 2 are queued'. It also means a persist failure now rejects the race inside the loop. Previously it surfaced only at the final `await persistChain`, after in-flight fetches had drained. The result is the same (the chunk throws), but it now abandons in-flight fetches mid-loop. This is acceptable; I would note the behaviour in the comment, or resolve a per-batch promise instead.

The `queuedPersists > MAX_QUEUED_PERSISTS` check is repeated in the launch loop condition and in `paused`, and `nextIndex < claimed.length && Date.now() < deadlineAt` is repeated too. Compute `canLaunchMore` once per iteration and derive `paused` from it, so the two conditions can't drift.

Adding pendingPersists to Promise.race makes a rejected persist throw out of the crawl loop immediately. Before, it surfaced only at `await persistChain` after in-flight fetches finished. The fail-fast looks acceptable because writes are idempotent and unattempted leases are reclaimed, but it is an unrequested side effect. Confirm it is intended, or note it in a comment.
`Math.min(byteCap, MAX_WINDOW, windowSize + 5)` repeats MAX_WINDOW, since byteCap is already capped at MAX_WINDOW. Use `Math.min(byteCap, windowSize + 5)`.

`await Promise.race([...inFlight, ...pendingPersists])` now observes persist promises directly. A rejected persist makes the race throw mid-loop, with fetches still in flight and unlaunched leases not yet released. Before, the failure surfaced only at `await persistChain` after the loop drained. Race on the settle-wrapped promises (`persist.then(settle, settle)` results) so the wait never rejects and error handling stays at the final `await persistChain`.
`Math.min(byteCap, MAX_WINDOW, windowSize + 5)`: `byteCap` is already capped at `MAX_WINDOW` and floored at `MIN_WINDOW`, so the `MAX_WINDOW` argument is redundant.

`persistChain` resolves only when the whole queue has drained, not when it falls to MAX_QUEUED_PERSISTS or below. With nothing in flight and a backed-up queue, the loop sits idle until every queued persist finishes, which loses some pipelining. The comment's 'persistence progress' overstates it. Resolve a waiter from the `finally` that decrements `queuedPersists`, or reword the comment.

Putting `persistChain` into the race means a persist rejection throws from the loop while fetches are still in flight and still pushing into `batch`. Before, the error surfaced only after the loop ended. This is probably fine because the step fails and retries either way, but it is a behaviour change. `canLaunchMore` also repeats the launch-loop conditions (`nextIndex < claimed.length && Date.now() < deadlineAt`); a small shared predicate would avoid the drift.
`canLaunch` is defined directly above `while (true)` with no blank line. Add a blank line, or move it next to `launch` with the other loop helpers.

`settled` is a self-referencing promise (it deletes itself from `queuedPersists` inside its own `.then`) with a swallow-both-branches `.then(() => undefined, () => undefined)`. It works but takes a few reads to follow. A simpler option is a `queuedPersists` counter decremented in a `.finally`, plus a stored 'next persist done' promise to race on. Optional.

`emptyPageResult` now requires `htmlBytes`, and two of its three callers pass a literal 0. Making it optional with a default of 0 would shrink the diff. Only the blocked/error path with a body needs to pass a real value. Fine to keep as is.

When the persist queue is above the limit and fetches are still in flight, the loop only wakes on Promise.race(inFlight). A persist-queue drain doesn't wake it, so one slow fetch can leave the window under-filled after the DB has caught up. Racing persistChain alongside inFlight would fix it. This is not a memory risk.
emptyPageResult now has a required htmlBytes field, and three of the four callers pass a literal 0. Make it optional with a default of 0 so only the blocked/error path passes a value.

htmlBytes is set from body.length, which counts UTF-16 code units, not bytes. The success path already did this. The budget comment in crawl-window.ts says bytes, so the difference is worth a short note.

`persistChain` is now part of `Promise.race` while paused, which changes error timing. A persist failure used to surface only at the final `await persistChain`. Now it rejects the race at once and leaves in-flight fetches running. The race also waits for the entire chain to finish, not just for the queue to drop to MAX_QUEUED_BATCHES or below. Both are probably acceptable, but state the intent in the comment or confirm that failing fast is wanted.

`persistChain` is now raced inside the crawl loop while launching is paused. If `persistCrawledPages` throws, `.then` skips every later batch's callback, so its `finally` never runs and `queuedBatches` stays above `MAX_QUEUED_BATCHES`. The loop is then paused with a rejected `persistChain`, so the race rejects and the chunk aborts while fetches are still in flight. Previously a persist error only surfaced at the final `await persistChain`. Aborting early is probably the right behaviour, but it is a silent change. Either say so in the comment, or make the accounting robust, for example by catching in the chain and rethrowing at the end.

The `htmlBytes` doc comment is now stale. It says the field is 'capped at MAX_HTML_BYTES' and 'feeds the crawl window's memory-pressure signal, since response time is measured at headers'. That described the removed heavy-page trouble check. The field now feeds the in-flight HTML byte budget and is also set on blocked and non-ok pages. Update the comment to match.

The `persisted`/`tracked` promise pair plus a `Set` with a self-deleting `then` is more machinery than the queue-depth check needs. A plain pending-count with a wake-up promise, or the count alone alongside `persistChain`, would be simpler to read. The `waitingOnPersist` condition also repeats the launch-loop conditions (`nextIndex`, deadline, queue size). It works as written, so this is optional.

`htmlBytes` is now a required field on `emptyPageResult`, so the redirect and catch call sites each pass an explicit `htmlBytes: 0`. Make it optional with a default of 0 so only the blocked/error site passes `body.length`.
The `htmlBytes` doc comment is stale. It describes a memory-pressure signal, but `htmlBytes` now feeds the in-flight byte budget and is also set for blocked and error pages. Reword it.

Racing `persisting` promises while paused changes when a persist failure surfaces. Previously a failed `persistCrawledPages` was only observed at the final `await persistChain`, after in-flight fetches had drained. Now `Promise.race` rejects mid-loop, and the chunk step throws while `crawlPage` fetches are still running and buffering bodies in the isolate. The step fails either way and retries, so this is low impact. Still, consider racing a rejection-swallowing wrapper such as `queued.catch(() => {})` for the wake-up, and let `await persistChain` report the error as before.

The `htmlBytes` doc comment is stale. It still says "capped at MAX_HTML_BYTES" and calls the field a memory-pressure signal for heavy pages. It now feeds the in-flight byte budget and is also set for blocked and error pages. Redirect, non-HTML and thrown-error pages still report 0, and the comment should say so.

`resolveMarketSelector` types its argument as `Pick<GetRankedKeywordsArgs, ...>` but is also called with `FindSerpCompetitorsArgs`. It only works because the two types happen to match structurally. An explicit `{ market?: Market; locationCode?: number; languageCode?: string }` parameter type would state the contract directly.

resolveMarketSelector computes the location-only language itself with getLanguageCode. resolveMarket (via resolveLabsMarket) already snaps the language to the location's default when it differs from the project's. The sibling tools get_domain_overview and get_domain_keyword_suggestions just call resolveLabsMarket(args, project) plus assertLabsLocationCode and assertLanguageForLocation. The extra rule makes these tools differ from the siblings: a Switzerland/fr project with locationCode 2756 and no language gives de here but fr in the siblings. Reuse the shared path, or document the deliberate difference.

The shared resolver is typed with Pick<GetRankedKeywordsArgs, ...>, tying it to one tool's args even though find_serp_competitors also calls it. An inline type of market, locationCode and languageCode says what it needs. This is optional.

The `market.country != null` branch is redundant. Passing a US/`en` project to `resolveLabsMarket` returns the same result as calling `resolveMarket` on it, because US/`en` is always Labs-served. Use `resolveLabsMarket(args, args.market?.country != null ? { locationCode: DEFAULT_LOCATION_CODE, languageCode: "en" } : project)`. That removes the `resolveMarket` import and the second path.

resolveMarketSelector re-implements the location/language defaulting that resolveMarket/resolveLabsMarket already provide. Sibling tools (get-domain-overview, get-domain-keyword-suggestions) call resolveLabsMarket(args, project) plus the two asserts. Only the legacy market.country → US/en case is special, so pass US/en as the explicit defaults in that case and call resolveLabsMarket otherwise, instead of a parallel ternary.

With locationCode alone, language is always getLanguageCode(locationCode), even when locationCode equals the project's location. resolveMarket keeps the project's language in that case, so a Switzerland/fr project passing locationCode 2756 gets de here but fr from get_domain_overview. Confirm this divergence is intended; reusing resolveLabsMarket would make the tools consistent.

resolveMarketSelector hand-rolls the 'explicit location → that location's primary language, else project language' rule that resolveMarket/resolveLabsMarket already implement (and that get-domain-overview and get-domain-keyword-suggestions call directly). Choose the base (US/en when legacy market.country is set, else project) and delegate: resolveLabsMarket(args, base), then assertLabsLocationCode + assertLanguageForLocation. This removes the getLanguageCode import and the inline nested ternary, and keeps language resolution consistent with sibling tools. It also avoids the divergence where passing the project's own locationCode keeps the project language in siblings but snaps to the location default here.

The `marketSchema` description says `market` is "Ignored when locationCode or languageCode is given". That is only true for `locationCode`. With `market` plus `languageCode` alone, `market` still sets the location to US and `languageCode` overrides only the language. The `languageCode` description also omits that `market` sets the location. Reword so the schema text matches the actual resolution.

The `marketSchema` description says `market` is 'Ignored when locationCode or languageCode is given', but that is only true for `locationCode`. With `market` plus only `languageCode`, `resolveMarketSelector` still uses the US base location, so the project's location is not used. Reword it, e.g. 'locationCode/languageCode override the matching parts of this selector'.

In resolveMarketSelector, the `market?.country != null` ternary picks between resolveMarket (with a US/en fallback) and resolveLabsMarket (with the project). Collapsing it to a single `resolveLabsMarket(args, market?.country != null ? { locationCode: DEFAULT_LOCATION_CODE, languageCode: 'en' } : project)` would give one resolver call and read more simply. Optional.

The ternary between `resolveMarket` and `resolveLabsMarket` can be flattened: `resolveLabsMarket(args, args.market?.country != null ? { locationCode: DEFAULT_LOCATION_CODE, languageCode: "en" } : project)`. The US fallback is Labs-served, so the result is the same, and it needs one resolver call and no `resolveMarket` branch. Optional.

resolveMarketSelector now repeats the resolveLabsMarket + assertLabsLocationCode + assertLanguageForLocation sequence that get-domain-overview.ts and get-domain-keyword-suggestions.ts also inline. Optionally extract one shared helper (e.g. in server/lib/market.ts) so the Labs-market validation can't drift between tools. Fine to defer.

`rankedLocationCodeSchema` and `rankedLanguageCodeSchema` are shared by `get_ranked_keywords` and `find_serp_competitors`, so the 'ranked' prefix is misleading. Something like `labsLocationCodeSchema` and `labsLanguageCodeSchema` would describe them better. Optional.

resolveMarketSelector packs the Zod-enum comment, a ternary and a destructure into one expression. Optional: pick the fallback (US when market.country is set, else project) in a plain if, then resolve and assert once. Behaviour is correct as written.

The nested ternary that builds `explicit` in `resolveMarketSelector` packs three cases into one expression. An early `if` for explicit fields and an `if` for the legacy US `market` would read more easily. Behaviour is correct, so this is optional.
